title: The accountant's report requirement
subtitle: Rule 12 of the SRA Accounts Rules 2019 — the annual check, and when it has to reach the SRA
objectives: State the annual accountant's report obligation under SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 12, including the six-month delivery window
Distinguish an unqualified report from a qualified report, and explain what happens to each
Apply the limited-client-money exemption to a fact pattern to determine whether a firm needs a report at all

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the annual accountant's report obligation, the delivery deadline, and the exemption for firms holding only limited client money

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students know 'firms holding client money need an accountant's report.' Where the profile shows the qualified/unqualified distinction and the exemption are shaky, this note appears: 'You know the report exists — this lesson is about what triggers it, what happens to it once it's made, and who's actually exempt.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well recalling the six-month deadline before. The test pool here leans on fact patterns about firm size, client money held, and report outcomes — not bare definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Parts 2 and 3 — the rest of the lesson assumes you can state the deadline and the qualified/unqualified distinction without hesitating.

overview.hook: Once a year, an accountant who has never met the firm's clients spends days going through its client ledgers, its reconciliations, and its bank statements, looking for exactly one thing: has this firm kept other people's money separate and safe, the way the rules require? Most reports end with a clean answer. Some don't — and what happens next depends entirely on which kind of answer it is.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The r 12 framework — including the six-month delivery window and the limited-client-money exemption — is the current SRA position; no change is pending, but accountant's report requirements have been narrowed by the SRA in recent years and are worth checking for further reform.

parts.heading: Why an outsider checks the books
parts.voice: argumentative — states the case for the requirement, then narrows it
body: Everything covered so far in this module — the correction duty, reconciliation, residual balances — depends on the firm policing itself. The accountant's report is the one external check layered on top: an independent qualified accountant examines the firm's client account records once a year and reports on whether the firm has, in essence, complied with the rules that keep client money separate and safe.

The justification is straightforward: client money sits in accounts the client themselves never sees, controlled entirely by the firm. Internal reconciliation catches errors the firm itself can spot; an external report exists to catch what internal processes might have missed, or covered up, because the person doing the checking isn't the person who did the bookkeeping.

But the obligation isn't universal. It applies to firms that hold or receive client money — and even then, a firm that holds only a genuinely limited amount of client money is exempted from needing a report at all. The rest of this lesson maps exactly where that line sits, and what the report actually does once it exists.

components.definition: An annual report by a qualified accountant, required of most firms that hold or receive client money, assessing the firm's compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules over the accounting period.

interaction.prompt: What is the basic purpose of the accountant's report requirement under r 12?
options: To calculate the firm's tax liability for HMRC
To give an independent, external check on the firm's compliance with the Accounts Rules over the year
To value the firm for the purposes of a partnership dispute
To replace the need for internal reconciliation entirely
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. It's an external, independent check — layered on top of, not a replacement for, the firm's own internal controls like reconciliation.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The report isn't about tax or valuation — it's an independent accountant's assessment of whether the firm has complied with the Accounts Rules over the relevant period.

parts.heading: Rule 12: the six-month deadline
body: Where a report is required, r 12 fixes the timetable: the firm must obtain an accountant's report and deliver it to the SRA within six months of the end of the accounting period it covers, where the rules require delivery at all — a point that matters more than it first appears, because delivery is not automatic for every report (more on that in Part 3).

The accounting period is usually the firm's own accounting reference date — the date its financial year ends — not a date set by the SRA. That means the six-month clock starts running from a date specific to each firm, so two firms can have completely different report deadlines depending on when their financial year happens to close.

Missing the deadline is not a technicality. A firm that fails to have a report prepared and, where required, delivered within the six-month window is in breach of r 12 regardless of whether the underlying accounts turn out to be perfectly clean.

components.text: You must obtain an accountant's report for each accounting period, unless the exception in r 12.2 applies. The report must be delivered to the SRA within six months of the end of the accounting period, where the accountant's report is qualified in accordance with guidance published by the SRA.
elements: A report is required for each accounting period, subject to the r 12.2 exemption
The accounting period generally runs to the firm's accounting reference date
Where delivery to the SRA is required, it must happen within six months of the end of that period

interaction.prompt: From what point does the six-month delivery window in r 12 run?
options: From the date the accountant is instructed
From the end of the firm's accounting period
From the date the SRA requests the report
From the date the firm's last reconciliation was carried out
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The clock runs from the end of the accounting period, which is why firms with different financial year-ends have different deadlines.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The trigger date is the end of the accounting period itself — not when the accountant starts work, or when the SRA happens to ask.

parts.heading: Unqualified and qualified: two very different outcomes
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the split before naming the doctrine
body: Not every accountant's report ends up in the SRA's hands. The single most important distinction in this area is between an unqualified report and a qualified report, because they trigger entirely different consequences.

An unqualified report is, in effect, a clean bill of health: the accountant found no material breaches significant enough to flag. The firm must obtain it and retain it — keeping it available for inspection — but there is no general requirement to actively send an unqualified report to the SRA as a matter of routine.

A qualified report is different: the accountant has identified breaches serious enough, in their professional judgement, to require reporting — typically involving matters that suggest client money may not be safe. A qualified report must be delivered to the SRA, and delivery is exactly what r 12's six-month deadline is aimed at. The distinction isn't a matter of degree the firm gets to weigh up; it's the accountant's own assessment of the report that decides which category it falls into.

components.label: Unqualified vs qualified reports
points: Unqualified: no material breaches significant enough to flag — obtained and retained by the firm, not routinely delivered to the SRA
Qualified: the accountant identifies breaches serious enough to require reporting — must be delivered to the SRA
The six-month deadline in r 12 is specifically aimed at delivery of a qualified report
It is the accountant's professional assessment, not the firm's own view, that determines which category applies

interaction.prompt: Which scenario describes a qualified report that must be delivered to the SRA?
interaction.scenarioA: The accountant reviews the firm's records, finds two minor, promptly-corrected transposition errors with no lasting impact, and issues a clean report with no matters flagged.
interaction.scenarioB: The accountant reviews the firm's records and finds a recurring pattern of client money being used to cover office account shortfalls, never fully corrected, across the year.
interaction.explanation: B describes exactly the kind of serious, unresolved breach that produces a qualified report requiring delivery to the SRA. A's minor, promptly-corrected errors are consistent with an unqualified report that the firm retains but need not routinely send in.

parts.heading: The limited-client-money exemption
parts.voice: explanatory — works through the narrow carve-out
body: Rule 12.2 exempts some firms from the accountant's report requirement altogether. The exemption is narrow and targeted: it applies to firms that hold or receive only a genuinely limited category of client money — most notably, money received that relates only to payments from the Legal Aid Agency, or certain other tightly defined categories the SRA treats as low-risk.

This is not a general small-firm exemption, and it is easy to over-read it as one. A small firm that routinely holds client money for conveyancing completions, for example, does not qualify simply because it is small — the exemption turns on the nature and limited scope of the money held, not the size of the practice.

The practical effect for an exempt firm is significant: no annual report obligation at all, which removes a real compliance cost. But the exemption doesn't touch anything else in this module — an exempt firm still owes the correction duty, still must reconcile its accounts, and still must deal properly with residual balances, wherever it does hold any client money.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume the exemption is about firm size — 'small firms don't need an accountant's report.'
components.whyItsWrong: The exemption in r 12.2 is about the limited nature of the client money held, not the size of the firm. A small firm holding ordinary client money for conveyancing or litigation still needs a report; a larger firm that happens to hold only a narrow, defined category of low-risk money could in principle be exempt.

interaction.prompt: A three-partner firm holds client money only in the form of Legal Aid Agency payments passed through to clients, and holds no other client money of any kind. Assess whether the firm needs an accountant's report.
factsToOrder: The firm holds client money only from Legal Aid Agency payments
The firm holds no other category of client money

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the firm is exempt from the accountant's report requirement under r 12.2.
modelAnswer.rule: Rule 12.2 exempts firms that hold or receive only a limited, defined category of client money — including money relating only to Legal Aid Agency payments — from the annual accountant's report requirement. The exemption turns on the nature of the money held, not the size of the firm.
modelAnswer.application: The firm's size is irrelevant to the exemption. What matters is that the only client money it holds falls within the narrow category the exemption covers — Legal Aid Agency payments — and it holds no other client money that would take it outside the exemption.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, the firm falls within the r 12.2 exemption and does not need to obtain an accountant's report, provided it genuinely holds no other category of client money.

parts.heading: Where students trip on this rule
body: The most common error is treating 'unqualified' as meaning 'no obligation at all.' It isn't — an unqualified report must still be obtained annually; the firm just isn't generally required to send it to the SRA. Skipping the report altogether because last year's was clean is a breach of r 12 in its own right.

A second common error is assuming every report, qualified or not, has to be delivered to the SRA as a matter of routine. It's specifically the qualified report that triggers the delivery obligation and the six-month deadline — an unqualified report is retained, available for inspection, not proactively filed.

A third error, already flagged in Part 4, is over-reading the limited-client-money exemption as a general small-firm carve-out. Exam questions often test this directly by describing a small firm holding ordinary client money and inviting the (wrong) inference that its size alone exempts it.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students sometimes conclude that because a firm's last report was unqualified, the firm can skip obtaining a report the following year if nothing seems to have changed.
components.whyItsWrong: The obligation to obtain a report (subject to the r 12.2 exemption) applies to each accounting period on its own terms. A clean report last year says nothing about this year, and does not suspend the annual requirement.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this firm has misunderstood what an unqualified report requires of it.
interaction.scenarioText: A firm obtained an unqualified accountant's report last year. This year, believing nothing has changed and the previous report was clean, the firm decides not to obtain a new report at all, and does not instruct an accountant.
tappableSpans: obtained an unqualified accountant's report last year
decides not to obtain a new report at all
interaction.correctSpan: decides not to obtain a new report at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The obligation to obtain a report applies each accounting period — a clean report last year doesn't exempt the firm from getting one this year.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the point where the firm actually skips a required step, rather than just its reasoning for doing so. The failure is not instructing an accountant at all for the new period.

testPool.prompt: Under r 12, within how many months of the end of the accounting period must a qualified accountant's report be delivered to the SRA?
options: Three months
Six months
Nine months
Twelve months
testPool.explanation: The delivery window for a qualified report is six months from the end of the accounting period it covers.

testPool.prompt: What is the basic difference between an unqualified and a qualified accountant's report?
options: An unqualified report is prepared by a trainee accountant, a qualified report by a partner
An unqualified report finds no significant breaches; a qualified report flags breaches serious enough to require SRA notification
An unqualified report covers office account only; a qualified report covers client account only
There is no meaningful difference — both must always be delivered to the SRA
testPool.explanation: Unqualified means clean, in substance; qualified means the accountant has found matters serious enough to flag, which triggers delivery to the SRA.

testPool.prompt: A firm receives an unqualified accountant's report for the year. What must the firm do with it?
options: Deliver it to the SRA within six months as a matter of routine
Obtain and retain it, without a general requirement to proactively deliver it to the SRA
Destroy it once the following year's report is obtained
Publish a summary of it to all current clients
testPool.explanation: An unqualified report must be obtained and kept available; it is the qualified report, not the unqualified one, that must generally be delivered to the SRA.

testPool.prompt: From what date does the six-month clock in r 12 begin running for a firm's accountant's report?
options: The date the firm instructs its reporting accountant
The end of the firm's accounting period
1 April each year, for all firms regardless of their own financial year-end
The date the SRA issues a formal request
testPool.explanation: The period runs from the end of the firm's own accounting period, which is why deadlines differ firm to firm depending on their financial year-end.

testPool.prompt: A four-partner high-street firm holds client money for house purchases and estate administration. It has fewer than ten fee earners. Does its small size exempt it from the accountant's report requirement?
options: Yes — firms below a certain headcount are automatically exempt under r 12.2
No — the r 12.2 exemption turns on the limited nature of the client money held, not the size of the firm
Yes — provided the firm's turnover is also below a set threshold
No — small firms are in fact subject to a stricter reporting requirement than larger ones
testPool.trapExplanation: Firm size feels like an intuitive basis for an exemption aimed at reducing compliance burden, but r 12.2 is drawn around the nature of the money held — this firm holds ordinary client money for conveyancing and probate, which is exactly the kind of money the exemption doesn't cover.
testPool.explanation: Holding client money for house purchases and estate administration is ordinary client money outside the narrow exemption — the firm needs a report regardless of its size.

testPool.prompt: A firm's accountant's report for the year was unqualified. The following year, believing the position is unlikely to have changed, the firm does not instruct an accountant to prepare a new report. Has the firm complied with r 12?
options: Yes — an unqualified report from the previous year is sufficient evidence of ongoing compliance
No — the obligation to obtain a report applies to each accounting period, regardless of the previous year's result
Yes — provided the firm's own internal reconciliations show no problems
No — but only because the firm should have delivered last year's unqualified report to the SRA
testPool.trapExplanation: A clean prior report feels like it should carry forward, but r 12 attaches to each accounting period separately. Skipping a year because last year was clean is itself a breach.
testPool.explanation: The requirement to obtain a report (subject to the r 12.2 exemption) is annual and period-specific — a good result last year doesn't satisfy this year's obligation.

testPool.prompt: An accountant preparing a firm's report finds two minor transposition errors, both corrected the same week they occurred, with no lasting shortfall. What is the most likely outcome?
options: A qualified report, because any error at all must be flagged to the SRA
An unqualified report, since the errors were minor and promptly corrected with no lasting impact
No report is required at all, because the errors were immaterial
A qualified report, delivered to the SRA within six months regardless of materiality
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to think any identified error automatically qualifies a report, but the qualification decision turns on the accountant's professional judgement of materiality and seriousness — minor, promptly-corrected slips are consistent with a clean, unqualified outcome.
testPool.explanation: Qualification reflects breaches serious enough to warrant reporting, not the mere existence of any error. Minor, quickly-fixed mistakes typically remain within an unqualified report.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following firms is most likely to fall within the r 12.2 exemption from the accountant's report requirement?
options: A firm holding client money only for Legal Aid Agency payments passed through to clients
A small two-partner firm holding modest amounts of client money for conveyancing
A firm that reconciles its accounts monthly rather than every five weeks
A firm that has never previously received a qualified report
testPool.trapExplanation: It's easy to assume the exemption tracks firm size or a clean compliance history, but neither of those is the actual test — the exemption is defined by the narrow, low-risk category of client money the firm holds.
testPool.explanation: The exemption applies where the client money held falls within specific, limited categories such as Legal Aid Agency payments — not by reference to firm size or reconciliation frequency or past compliance record.

testPool.prompt: A firm's accounting period ends on 31 December. Its accountant's report for that period is qualified. By what date must the firm deliver that report to the SRA?
options: 30 June the same year
30 June the following year
31 December the following year
There is no fixed deadline once a report is qualified
testPool.explanation: Six months from 31 December is 30 June of the following year — that is the deadline for delivering a qualified report to the SRA.

testPool.prompt: A firm holds client money for conveyancing matters and also, separately, holds Legal Aid Agency payments passed through to a small number of clients. Does the r 12.2 exemption apply?
options: Yes — because some of the money held falls within the exempt category
No — the exemption requires that the firm hold only the limited, defined categories of client money; holding conveyancing money as well takes the firm outside it
Yes — provided the Legal Aid Agency money exceeds the conveyancing money in value
No — Legal Aid Agency payments are never treated as client money for this purpose
testPool.explanation: The exemption is for firms holding only the limited category of money it covers. Holding any ordinary client money alongside it, such as conveyancing funds, takes the firm outside the exemption entirely.

testPool.prompt: A firm obtains an unqualified accountant's report and retains it on file, without sending it to the SRA. Six months after its accounting period ended, the SRA has still not received anything from the firm. Is the firm in breach of r 12?
options: Yes — every report must be delivered to the SRA within six months regardless of outcome
No — an unqualified report does not generally require delivery to the SRA; retaining it is sufficient
Yes — but only because six months have now passed
No — because the six-month deadline only applies to firms exempt under r 12.2
testPool.explanation: The six-month delivery deadline is specifically tied to a qualified report. An unqualified report, properly obtained and retained, does not trigger a routine delivery obligation.

testPool.prompt: Reading r 12 as a whole, what is the relationship between the obligation to obtain a report and the obligation to deliver one to the SRA?
options: They are the same obligation, triggered at the same time for every firm
Obtaining a report is the general annual obligation; delivery to the SRA is an additional step that arises specifically where the report is qualified
Delivery to the SRA is the general obligation; obtaining the report is optional
Neither obligation applies unless the firm has previously received a qualified report
testPool.explanation: Rule 12 layers two distinct steps: obtaining a report each accounting period (subject to the r 12.2 exemption), and delivering it to the SRA, which is specifically required where the report is qualified.

testPool.prompt: What does r 12.2 provide for firms holding only a narrow, defined category of client money, such as Legal Aid Agency payments?
options: A reduced six-month deadline becomes a twelve-month deadline
An exemption from the requirement to obtain an accountant's report at all
A requirement to obtain two reports per year instead of one
No change — the same requirement applies regardless of the type of client money held
testPool.explanation: Rule 12.2 exempts firms holding only the specified limited categories of client money from the accountant's report requirement altogether.

testPool.prompt: A firm's accountant issues a qualified report on 1 May, covering an accounting period that ended on 31 January the same year. Has the firm met the r 12 delivery deadline if it delivers the report to the SRA on 20 July?
options: Yes — 20 July is within six months of 31 January
No — the deadline is six months from the date the report was issued, not from the end of the accounting period
Yes — because the report itself was ready well within six months of the period end
No — 20 July falls outside the six-month window measured from 31 January
testPool.explanation: Six months from 31 January is 31 July. Delivery on 20 July falls within that window, measured from the end of the accounting period, not from the date the accountant happened to sign the report.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring mistake in this lesson's test items is collapsing three separate questions into one: whether a report is needed at all (the r 12.2 exemption, about the type of money held, not firm size), whether it must be delivered to the SRA (only if qualified), and by when (six months from the end of the accounting period, not from any other date).
